### PR 6 — compaction rungs 1–2 + ceiling error (2026-08-20)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-20 | Shipped PR 6 BEFORE PR 5 (Vertex), at the user's instruction. The two are independent — compaction touches only `agent-aisdk-runner/src/compaction/` plus five lines of `main.ts`, and the Vertex work is a `PROVIDERS` entry plus a credential kind. | Recorded so the sequencing table in the design doc is not read as a claim about what merged. Nothing in PR 6 assumes a provider set. | — |
| 2026-08-20 | Compaction is a SEND-SITE transform only: `prepareStep` rewrites the messages for the request and the in-memory transcript is never touched. | Same rule the §6 reasoning prune already follows. The transcript's serialized bytes are the host's source of truth — rewriting them changes the shipped prefix, breaks `prefixHash`, and forces a whole-file resync on every resume; it would also make the compaction irreversible for the display history the UI renders. Rungs 1-2 are deterministic pure functions of the message list, so recomputing them every step costs nothing and needs no persisted state. (Rung 3, summarize, is the one that genuinely needs `session.replace-transcript` — it costs an LLM call and cannot be recomputed for free. That is PR 7's problem.) | Persist the compacted list via `session.replace-transcript` (rejected for rungs 1-2 — pays the durability cost of rung 3 with none of its need). |
| 2026-08-20 | **Deviation from design §7's "no tokenizer needed":** a tokenizer-free ESTIMATOR ships as a fallback signal (`compaction/estimate.ts`). | §7 says the provider reports `usage.inputTokens` every step, which is true — but only from the SECOND step. `agent.stream()` is a fresh call per turn, so step 0 of EVERY turn has `steps: []` and no reported usage. Without a fallback, the first request of every turn goes out uncompacted, which is exactly the request a resumed long conversation dies on (the stored transcript keeps growing while the sent one does not, so on a fresh process the first send is the biggest one). The estimator is never the primary signal: reported usage wins whenever it exists, and relative reductions are applied as a RATIO to the reported number so the arithmetic inherits the provider's accuracy. | Carry a usage watermark forward across turns in the loop (rejected — accurate within a process but absent after a resume in a fresh pod, which is the case that matters, and it is a second mechanism for the same job). Ship without a step-0 signal (rejected — the feature would not fire on the request it exists for). |
| 2026-08-20 | The ceiling error fires ONLY on a provider-reported number, never on an estimate. | Ending a conversation is the most destructive thing this code can do, and doing it on the strength of a chars-per-token guess is the worst available false positive. When only the estimate says "hopeless", we send the fully compacted prompt anyway: either it fits, or the provider's own context-length error says so in its own words — a strictly better failure than ours. | Throw on either signal (rejected — false positives kill live conversations). Never throw, always let the provider error (rejected — the provider's error names no remedy, and design §7 asks for a clean ceiling). |
| 2026-08-20 | Rung 2 uses `pruneMessages`' `toolCalls` knob but deliberately NOT its `reasoning` knob, even though design §7 lists reasoning pruning under rung 2. | Two reasons. (1) Invariant 4: `messagesForProvider` in provider.ts already owns reasoning policy per provider (§6); a second owner would be free to disagree. (2) It would be actively wrong mid-turn — the SDK's `before-last-message` spares only the LITERAL last message, which during a tool loop is the tool RESULT, so it would strip the reasoning from the assistant message holding the `tool_use`. Anthropic's thinking blocks are signed and required in exactly that position. Verified against ai@7.0.70's implementation, not the docs. | Prune reasoning here too (rejected — strips the signed block next to a tool_use). Move all reasoning policy into the compactor (rejected — the send-site transform must still run for turns that never compact). |
| 2026-08-20 | The context-window table lives in `agent-aisdk-runner/src/compaction/context-window.ts`, NOT in `@ax/core` next to `PROVIDER_ENDPOINTS`. | `PROVIDER_ENDPOINTS` is shared because two sides of the sandbox wall must AGREE on it and drift surfaces as a MITM 403. Nothing on the host reads a context window — it is consumed here and only here, so a shared copy would be a second source of truth bought for nothing (invariant 4). Also considered and rejected: reading OpenRouter's real `context_length` from `GET /api/v1/models` — a boot-path network call, against the egress allow-list, for a number that changes when a model ships rather than per session. | Put it in `@ax/core` (rejected — no second reader; move it when one appears). Fetch it from OpenRouter at boot (rejected — new boot-path failure mode for a static fact). |
| 2026-08-20 | Anthropic's entry is a provider-wide 200k FALLBACK with an empty per-model map; OpenRouter's is per-model with a conservative 128k fallback. | Every shipping Claude model is 200k, so the fallback handles the case a per-model map handles worst: a model released after the table was written. OpenRouter fronts hundreds of models across every size class, so there is no honest provider-wide number. Guessing low costs some old tool output; guessing high is backstopped by the provider's own error. | Enumerate every model on both sides (rejected — rots, and rots silently). |

### PR 7 — compaction rung 3 (summarize) + the eval bench (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | **Rung 3 fires at the TURN BOUNDARY (`compactor.turn()`, called from main.ts before `agent.stream()`), not as a third rung inside `prepareStep`.** Design §7 reads as one ladder in one place; it is two entry points on one object. | `prepareStep` may return a promise, so an LLM call there is mechanically possible — it is still wrong. (1) Mid-tool-loop the newest messages are a live `tool_use`/`tool_result` pair plus, on Anthropic, a signed thinking block that must be replayed in position; splicing a synthetic message into that region is a 400, not a degradation. (2) There is no quiescent moment to persist — `session.replace-transcript` mid-step publishes a transcript whose newest half is a half-finished step. At the turn boundary every tool call has its result and the rewrite is durable before a token of the new turn is spent. Step 0 of a resumed long conversation — the request PR 6's estimator exists for — happens immediately AFTER this, so the case that matters is covered. | Async rung 3 inside `prepareStep` (rejected — pairing + no persist point). Both sites (rejected — double the surface and the failure modes to cover a single runaway turn, which the 0.9 ceiling already ends cleanly). |
| 2026-08-21 | Rung 3's trigger is 0.75 of the window measured on the conversation AFTER a hypothetical rung 1 + rung 2, not on the conversation as stored. | This is what makes the ladder cheapest-first ACROSS the two entry points. Measured as stored, rung 3 would buy a model call for a conversation whose bulk is one turn's tool output — exactly what mask and prune reclaim for free a moment later at the send site. Asking the pure functions "what will you manage on your own?" is cheaper and more honest than guessing. | Trigger on the stored size (rejected — pays for a summary the free rungs would have made unnecessary). Share `COMPACT_AT` (rejected — the two rungs would fire together and the ordering would be meaningless). |
| 2026-08-21 | The turn boundary has no reported usage, so `turn()` uses the estimator scaled by a CALIBRATION — the ratio of the last provider-reported `inputTokens` to the estimator's number for the same request, learned in `step()`. | Extends PR 6's "reported wins, estimator supplies ratios" one step further out. The two message lists differ by one step's worth of messages, which on a conversation large enough to reach this threshold is a small fraction — so this is a calibration, not a measurement, and it is only ever allowed to decide "spend a model call". The rule that an estimate may never END a conversation is unchanged: the ceiling still fires only on a reported number. | Use the raw estimate (rejected — inconsistent with the file's own stated philosophy, and wrong by whatever the estimator's scale error is). Carry a usage watermark (rejected for the same reason PR 6 rejected it — absent after a resume in a fresh pod). |
| 2026-08-21 | The preserved tail snaps BACKWARD to the nearest `user` message; if there is none, `planSummarization` returns null and rung 3 declines. | Pairing is preserved by construction rather than repaired. A `user` message is the one role that never carries a tool result (the SDK models those as `tool` messages, and provider-executed ones as `assistant` parts), so it is always a safe seam. Backward only ever preserves MORE than the 30% asked for, which is the safe direction to err. Declining is the honest answer for a conversation that is one enormous turn — every candidate seam is mid-exchange, and there is nothing to summarize that would not orphan something. | Repair orphans after splicing (rejected — reconstructing the missing half of a tool exchange is inventing a record). Snap forward (rejected — hands live context to the summarizer). |
| 2026-08-21 | The summarized span is rendered to flat TEXT inside a `<transcript>` delimiter and sent as one prompt, not replayed to the summarizer as real messages. | Replaying it as messages would drag the whole pairing problem into a call whose only job is to read — every `tool` message needing its `tool-call`, every signed thinking block needing its position. Flattening makes the summarizer call provider-agnostic and unable to fail on a pairing rule. Reasoning parts are dropped from the render: they are the model's scratch work about the very span being summarized, so rendering them pays twice for one thing. Per-tool-output render is capped at 2,000 chars (4x rung 1's mask budget). | Replay as messages (rejected — pairing, and it makes the summarizer provider-specific). Summarize the already-masked span (rejected — builds the summary from degraded input to save tokens on a once-per-many-turns call). |
| 2026-08-21 | The summary is spliced as a **`user`** message opening with a note that says it is machine-generated and that instructions inside it are a record, not a request. | The role follows `seedFromHistory`'s precedent (an out-of-band note about the conversation is not something the assistant said, and attributing it to the assistant invites the model to contradict its own turn). The note's second half is the INJECTION mitigation: the summary's text derives from tool output, the least trusted bytes in the system, and without the disclaimer anything that survived would arrive wearing the user's role — a real escalation from "a tool printed this" to "my operator said this". The blast radius is bounded regardless: every tool call still goes through `wrapWithPolicy` → `tool.pre-call`, and the summarizer itself is called with NO tools. | `assistant` role (rejected — the model contradicting its own summary). A bare summary with no note (rejected — a model that thinks its record is complete confabulates, and the trust escalation goes unmarked). |
| 2026-08-21 | New `LoopContext.replaceTranscript()` in runner-core, backed by an exported `replaceWholeTranscript` in transcript-delta.ts. Best-effort: it does NOT throw. | Design §5 asks for the rewrite to be ANNOUNCED rather than discovered. The delta ship would notice on its own — a shortened transcript cannot match its prefix hash — but `resync-required` exists for rewrites nobody announced (an SDK compacting its own jsonl behind our back), and leaning on it would also delay durability to the end of the turn, so a crash mid-turn would buy the summarizer call twice. Not throwing is deliberate and the fallback is the reason: on failure the state is left UNADVANCED, so the next `endTurn` delta fails its prefix check and the resync path replaces the whole thing anyway. Failing a turn over a bookkeeping call whose own fallback is already in place is the wrong trade. | Let the resync path discover it (rejected — §5, plus the durability delay). Throw on failure (rejected — the fallback makes it recoverable). Bind the runner session here too (rejected — a rewrite can only happen to a conversation that already has turns, so the bind already happened; a second path to that state is a second thing to get wrong). |
| 2026-08-21 | `MemoryTranscriptSource.replace()` keeps an entry's uuid when the message is the SAME OBJECT, by identity, not by deep equality. | The uuid is what `lastUuidOfRole` reports as the host's `turnId`, which the display log and `conversations:drop-turn` already point at. Re-minting uuids for messages that did not change would orphan those references. Identity rather than structural equality because two turns that say the same thing are two turns, and collapsing them would make two rows share one id. Rung 3 passes head and tail through by reference precisely so this holds — the summarize unit suite asserts the reference-passing, because "we were careful" is not a mechanism. | Deep-equality matching (rejected — collides on repeated turns). Re-mint everything (rejected — orphans live turn ids). |
| 2026-08-21 | §7's "do not retry in a loop" is implemented in TWO forms: one attempt per turn (no in-attempt retry), and a cross-turn backoff — after a failure, rung 3 is not attempted again until the message count has grown 25%. | The in-attempt rule is what §7 literally says. The cross-turn rule is the same rule one level out: a deterministic failure (a summarizer that keeps producing something larger than the span) would otherwise buy a model call at the top of every remaining turn and change nothing. Growth is the signal that the input is materially different from the one that failed. A success resets the counter, so one bad turn does not disable the rung. | Disable rung 3 permanently after one failure (rejected — punishes a transient network blip with a permanently degraded session). No backoff (rejected — a real bill for a repeated no-op). |
| 2026-08-21 | The eval bench (`test/bench/`) runs a **`verbatim` control arm** and gates on the DELTA (`recallLoss`), not on the compacted arm's absolute score. With no control arm the gate FAILS rather than falling back to the absolute. | §7 asks whether a question is still answerable AFTER compaction — a claim about what compaction COST, not about how good the model is at reading a long transcript. Some needles the model gets wrong from the full conversation too; charging those to compaction makes the gate a measure of the filler's difficulty instead. Failing rather than falling back because a gate that silently changes meaning is worse than no gate. Confabulation is reported separately and held to a stricter bar (10% vs 25%): a summary that loses a fact and admits it is a much better failure than one that invents a replacement, and the two call for opposite fixes. | Gate on the compacted arm alone (rejected — measures the corpus, not the transform). Fold confabulation into recall (rejected — one number cannot carry two failures with opposite remedies). |
| 2026-08-21 | The corpus is generated, its facts carry an explicit `token` string, and the driver THROWS if any token is found in the preserved head/tail (or missing from the summarized middle). | Answering "does this transform destroy facts a later turn needs" requires knowing what the facts are and where they sit, which no corpus of real sessions gives. The fairness check is the part that matters: a fact in the preserved region survives by construction and would be scored as recall through a summary it never went through. An earlier version extracted the token from the gold answer with a heuristic — replaced, because a heuristic that quietly returns nothing turns the check off without saying so, and a rigged bench is worse than a broken one (a broken one gets fixed). | Heuristic token extraction (rejected — silent failure disables the check). No fairness check (rejected — the score would be free). |

### Agent-workspace prototype — the approvals/attendance model (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | `ask` does NOT become a blocking verdict. `tool.pre-call` gains a third NON-BLOCKING verdict `hold` that returns as fast as `reject`; the waiting (when there is anyone to wait for) happens one level up on `session.next-message`. | `IPC_TIMEOUTS_MS['tool.pre-call']` is **10 s** (`ipc-protocol/src/timeouts.ts:12`) and `tool-policy.ts:70` converts ANY failure of that call — timeout included — into `{decision:'deny'}`. So a human can never be waited for inside pre-call: blowing the ceiling produces a denial the model then improvises around, which is the worst possible outcome for "a human must see this first". Raising the ceiling would poison the hot path every tool call crosses. `hold` is still worth adding as distinct from `deny` because `deny` invites a workaround (different tool, shell command) while `hold` means "recorded, do not retry, tell the user, end the turn". | A blocking `ask` verdict (rejected — idle sandbox against the 6 h ceiling + idle reaper, for a decision made after lunch). Reuse `reject` with a magic reason string (rejected — the runner cannot distinguish "you may not" from "not yet", so the model routes around it). |
| 2026-08-21 | **Attendance**, not trigger source, decides the execution path. A Decision row is written in BOTH cases; the only difference is whether the runner parks. Attended → agent stays warm and executes its own call on approval. Unattended → turn ends, host replays the recorded `ToolCall` through `tool.execute-host`. | The user's insight: chatting live and a 3am routine fire are not the same situation. Modelling it as one axis keeps ONE durable row (invariant 4) with three renderers — the in-thread card, the Today queue, and eventually Slack buttons — and makes degradation automatic: when the reaper gives up on an attended park, the identical row is simply waiting in Today. No special case for "the user walked away mid-approval". | Two separate mechanisms for live vs background approvals (rejected — two sources of truth for one concept). Always replay (rejected — pays a cold start and a staleness risk in the case where the agent is demonstrably still alive). Always re-enter the model (rejected — gives up the WYSIWYG guarantee for the common case). |
| 2026-08-21 | Attendance is a property of the CHANNEL plus a park budget, not a boolean about routines. Web parks briefly; **Slack parks long** (interactive buttons resolve via `session.next-message`, same code path as a web click); routine tick and webhook do not park. | Chosen by the user over treating Slack as unattended-with-notification. Keeps Slack conversations continuous at the cost of a longer warm sandbox, and the existing idle→cancel→kill reaper already bounds that cost — an over-long Slack wait degrades into the queue exactly like an abandoned web thread. | Slack as unattended-with-notification (rejected by the user — breaks conversational continuity in Slack). |
| 2026-08-21 | Approving an unattended decision runs a **freshness guard** before executing: a predicate captured at hold-time (thread head id, calendar slot etag, doc revision) is re-checked, and on mismatch the decision RE-OPENS with what changed instead of executing. On re-open the predicate is re-captured so a second approval proceeds. | A decision drafted at 7am and approved at 1pm may be approving a world that no longer exists — the hole in the first version of this design, which sold WYSIWYG replay while hiding staleness. Silent staleness is the failure mode that ends trust in the whole surface; "annoying but honest" wins. Scoped to the unattended path only: attended approvals resolve in seconds. | Execute regardless and let the user notice afterwards (rejected — the one failure this surface cannot afford). Always re-enter the model to re-check (rejected as the default — costs a turn and breaks the byte-identical guarantee; kept as the option for multi-call/judgment-bound actions). |
| 2026-08-21 | Approved and dismissed outcome strings are BOTH stored on the decision; neither is derived from the other. | The Claude Design prototype built the dismissed line by regexing the approved one, producing "You took over from Inbox — sent your reply to Priya" for a reply that was never sent. A factual claim about what happened must never be the output of string surgery. Locked by `mock/__tests__/decision-machine.test.ts`. | Derive one from the other (rejected — see above). |
| 2026-08-21 | The permissions rail ("What it may do alone") is GENERATED from the policy record and each row carries the rule that produced it; a row whose sentence cannot be generated renders as an explicit "no rule mapped" warning rather than being omitted. | A UI that overstates or understates blast radius is the worst bug an autonomy surface can ship, and hand-authored sentences drift from enforced policy silently. Note `@ax/host-grants` is NOT the source — it is network hosts only (`{host, agentId, grantedAt}`); these are tool-policy semantics. An omitted capability reads to a user as "it cannot do that", which is the dangerous direction to be wrong in. | Hand-author the sentences (rejected — drifts, and the drift is invisible). Omit unmapped capabilities (rejected — silently understates reach). |
| 2026-08-21 | No progress bar, no ETA anywhere. "Right now" shows a real loop counter (`29 of 41 messages`) plus elapsed-since-start. | An LLM agent cannot know how long it has left, and one wrong "~2 min left" costs more trust than the widget can earn. Elapsed is knowable; remaining is not. | Keep the mockup's `pct` + `eta` (rejected — both are fabricated numbers on a surface whose entire value proposition is honesty). |
| 2026-08-21 | One event stream, one renderer. `ActivityFeed` is used by the global Activity page and by the per-agent "What it did" tab (`agentId` prop); Today's "Done" filter was cut, its reassurance moved into the digest sub-line, and the footer links into Activity. | The design had three components rendering the same rows — invariant 4 violated in the UI layer, and exactly the shape that drifts. The filter pod also mixed units (decisions / agents / events in one segmented control); it is now decisions and agents only. | Keep all three (rejected). |
| 2026-08-21 | The Today headline is TEMPLATED FROM COUNTS, never model-generated prose. | "Nothing has gone wrong" being wrong once ends the relationship. Every claim on the surface is derived from rows that were counted. | LLM-written digest (rejected — highest-risk sentence on the page). |
| 2026-08-21 | Memory is split by OWNER into "Rules you gave me" (human, verbatim, never rewritten) and "What it worked out" (agent, subject to rollup/GC), each labelled with who owns it. | The mockup put both under one editor promising "anything you write here sticks" — false for the agent-owned half, and a user whose hand-written note gets eaten by the strata GC does not forgive it. | One editor over all memory files (rejected). |
| 2026-08-21 | The prototype lives at `/workspace` in `packages/channel-web` behind `AGENT_WORKSPACE_PREVIEW = import.meta.env.DEV`, as REAL client code (shadcn, semantic tokens, lucide, HTTP fetch) standing on the existing Vite mock backend (`mock/server.ts`). | Makes "implementable once P1–P5 land" literal: the swap is deleting `mock/workspace.ts` and repointing `src/lib/workspace-api.ts`, not a rewrite. Honours invariant 6 (no separate Vite SPA, no ported hex palette, no Font Awesome). Not half-wired: it is a dev-gated design artifact with its own data, and in a prod build the route falls through to the normal chat shell. | Standalone published Artifact (rejected by the user — throwaway, re-derives the design system). A scratch Vite app (rejected — violates invariant 6). |
| 2026-08-21 | Added a `warning` semantic token trio (`--warning`, `--warning-foreground`, `--warning-soft`) to `index.css` + `tailwind.config.ts`. | "Held for a human" is a genuine third state that is neither an error (destructive) nor business as usual (primary), and the palette had no honest slot for it. A semantic token, not a raw `bg-amber-500`, keeps invariant 6 intact. | Reuse destructive (rejected — a held decision is not a failure). Raw Tailwind amber (rejected — invariant 6 forbids raw colour values). |
| 2026-08-21 | AW-1 inventory: connectors render as §4.3.4 GRANT ROWS derived from the connector record (`name` + `allowedHosts`), NOT as per-operation capability clauses. | Design §4.3.3 asserts "a connector manifest supplies its own `capability` clause per exposed operation". No such field exists: `Connector` (`connectors/src/types.ts:204-233`) has one `description` + one model-facing `usageNote` for the WHOLE connector; `Capabilities` (`skills-parser/src/capabilities.ts:50-67`) is hosts/credentials/mcpServers/packages/services with no operation list; `McpServerSpec` has no `tools`; the zod mirrors are `.strict()` so nothing can be smuggled in. Connectors have no concept of an "exposed operation" at all — reach is hosts + credential slots. Worse, nothing is positioned to READ such a field: the proxy sees bytes, `connectors:resolve` runs before the turn. | Add the field now (rejected — schema change across two packages that deliberately re-declare rather than import, plus an operator editor, plus a reader that doesn't exist; its own card). |
| 2026-08-21 | `PolicyRule.match` ships as `{ tool: string }` in AW-3; `when?: PredicateSpec` is DEFERRED until a rule earns it. | AW-1 opened all 20 enforcement points: NOT ONE keys on a predicate over tool input — every describable condition matches on the tool NAME alone. §4.3.1's `when?` has zero day-one users. The prototype's fixture sources (`gmail.send · intent=scheduling`, `calendar.move_event · attendees>1`) are exactly the predicate-shaped rules that do not exist. YAGNI per the plan's own audit rule. | Ship `when?` speculatively (rejected — dead code in the one file the whole rail depends on). |
| 2026-08-21 | AW-4's canary uses a `hold` rule on `request_capability`, not on `skill_propose` (the plan's example) and not on `Bash`. | `@ax/skill-broker` is pushed UNCONDITIONALLY into the k8s preset (`presets/k8s/src/index.ts:990`), so `request_capability` is always in the catalog, and it is `executesIn:'host'` → AW-5's `tool.execute-host` replay works. `skill_propose` is `executesIn:'sandbox'` (`tool-skill-propose/src/descriptor.ts:82`) so the host CANNOT replay it — a hold there is executable only on the attended path — and it is gated behind `AX_ALLOW_USER_INSTALLED_SKILLS`. `Bash` would fire on every command. | `skill_propose` (rejected — sandbox-executed + env-gated); `Bash` (rejected — unusable blast radius). |

### TASK-229 — the "Right now" line at T0/T1 (`@ax/agent-activity`) (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | T0's trigger label rides on the context as `AgentContext.triggerLabel`, NOT resolved through `routines:list` as AW-8's plan assumed. | The plan's route is unworkable: `routines:list` is keyed by `(agentId, path)` and nothing tells you WHICH routine is mid-flight. The only conversationId→routine join is the `FireRow`, and `@ax/routines` writes it at `chat:turn-end` — after the turn a label would have described. So the label has to ride on the context that starts the work. `triggerLabel` sits next to the existing `source: 'routine' \| 'user'`, is optional, human-authored, display-only, and carries no transport/storage vocabulary. `fire.ts` sets it to `row.name`. | Join through the conversation's title (rejected — for a `shared` routine the title is only the fallback at create time, and `@ax/conversation-titles` rewrites it afterwards, so the "label" would be model-generated prose). Stuff it in `ctx.state` under a magic key (rejected — cross-plugin coupling by string, with none of a field's reviewability). |
| 2026-08-21 | `deriveActivity` ships with the full counter contract, but NOTHING produces a `reported` count yet — so no counter renders. `countable` is the unit half only. | There is no tool-progress channel in the repo (no `tool:progress` hook, no progress field on any tool hook), and inventing `done`/`total` from a tool's input or output would be exactly the estimated number the design forbids. The rule lives in one pure function (`reported` + `countable` ⇒ counter; anything else ⇒ null), which is what the acceptance criterion actually constrains. A follow-up card takes the reporting channel. | Add `agent-activity:report-progress` with no caller (rejected — half-wired). Infer a total from an array-shaped tool input (rejected — the tool did not state it, so it is our guess wearing the tool's voice). |
| 2026-08-21 | Staleness keeps `source` at the tier the line HAD resolved to, and `stale: true` is the sole discriminator. | `source` is documented as provenance for debugging and for the tier fallback, not as the author of `phrase`. Blanking it on staleness would throw away the one fact a debugger wants ("what went quiet"). The type comment says so explicitly so no consumer reads `source` as authorship. | Force `source` to a fourth value on staleness (rejected — invents a tier that does not exist). |
| 2026-08-21 | The per-agent record caches the scoped tool catalog for the duration of ONE stretch of work, and throws it away at `chat:end`. | `tool:list` seals on first call and never changes afterwards, and it is filtered per calling agent — so a per-record cache is both correct under multi-tenancy and bounded by the number of agents actually working. A process-global cache would answer agent B out of agent A's scope; no cache would put a `session:get-config` lookup on every tool call for the sake of a status line. | Global name→phrase map (rejected — cross-tenant scope bleed). ### AW-2 / TASK-223 — the `hold` verdict, end to end (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | `Hold` is a **subtype of `Rejection`**, not a third arm of `FireResult`. | `FireResult<P>` has 67 consumers. A three-arm union forces every one of them to handle a case only `tool:pre-call` can produce, and the mechanical fix at each site (`else` → deny) is exactly what the subtype gives for free. The cost — `hold` is *structurally* a rejection everywhere except the one handler that reads `.hold` — is accepted deliberately, because that default is the fail-closed one. Revisit if a second hook ever needs to hold. | Widen `FireResult` (rejected — 67 mechanical edits for one producer). A separate `tool:pre-call-hold` hook (rejected — two hooks voting on one call is two sources of truth). |
| 2026-08-21 | `tool-pre-call.ts` checks `isHold(result)` **before** the generic `result.rejected` branch. | Both are `rejected: true`. Checking rejection first flattens a hold into a deny — precisely the outcome `hold` exists to prevent, since a deny invites the model to route around it. Order is load-bearing, so a test asserts the hold arm and not just the reject arm. | Check `.hold` inside the rejection branch (equivalent, but the guard is easier to delete by accident). |
| 2026-08-21 | On the aisdk runner `holdLatch` is **required** on `WrapWithPolicyOptions` and on all four tool-builder option types, not optional as the plan wrote it. | There the latch is load-bearing: `stopWhen` reads it, and a tool wired with no latch (or its own) would hold without stopping the turn — the silent-failure shape this repo has been bitten by. Required-typing makes a missing wire a compile error at every call site; a `HOLD_LATCH` symbol on the wrapped `execute` lets one test assert every tool in the real merged tool set shares the SAME instance by identity. Optional is kept on the claude-sdk adapter, where `continue:false` does the stopping and the latch only records WHICH decision stopped the turn. | Optional everywhere per the plan (rejected — a forgotten wire fails silently). Hang the latch off `ToolPolicy` (rejected — the policy is shared with the other runner, where the latch means something different). |
| 2026-08-21 | The claude-sdk adapter emits `{continue:false, stopReason}` **and** `permissionDecision:'deny'` together. | Belt and braces, not redundancy: `continue:false` is the SDK's clean stop, and the deny guarantees the tool does not execute in any SDK version that honours `continue` late. | `continue:false` alone (rejected — trusts an SDK ordering detail with a side effect we cannot undo). |
| 2026-08-21 | `note` is **host-authored only**. Model output must never reach it. | `note` flows host → model and is rendered to the user as a permissions message. Model-derived text in it would be a prompt-injection channel into exactly the sentence a human relies on to decide. The wire schema bounds it (`min(1).max(2000)`); `@ax/decisions` (TASK-225) must author it from the policy rule's own text. | Let a subscriber echo tool arguments into `note` (rejected — injection sink). |
| 2026-08-21 | `HookBus.fire` SPREADS a subscriber's rejection (`{...result, source: result.source ?? sub.plugin}`) instead of rebuilding it. | The rebuild dropped every field a `Rejection` subtype added. Fixing it only for `Hold` would re-arm the identical trap for the next subtype; spreading is correct by construction and costs nothing. `source` stays defaulted so an unattributed veto is still attributed to the subscriber that raised it. | Re-attach `.hold` specifically (rejected — fixes one case and leaves the trap). |
| 2026-08-21 | `assertAllToolsWrapped(tools, expectedLatch)` verifies hold-latch IDENTITY at boot, not just in a test. | A tool holding on its own latch is policy-wrapped, so the old assertion passed it — and at runtime the call would be refused while the turn carried on to the next step. Nothing throws, nothing logs. The repo's own rule is "enforce at boot, don't assert in prose", and `POLICY_WRAPPED` already sets that precedent one line away. The `expectedLatch` argument is optional so the existing unit tests of the wrapper stay unchanged. | Rely on the identity unit test + required-typing alone (rejected — both check the builders, neither checks the assembled set at boot). |
| 2026-08-21 | The claude-sdk turn-boundary drain is a named `drainHoldLatch(latch)` in `@ax/agent-runner-core`, not two lines inline. | The ORDER is the whole point and the wrong order is silent: reset before read and the caller always sees `null`, the hold is never recorded, and every existing test still passes. A named function with its own test makes that un-mis-writable. | Two lines at the call site (rejected — the reviewer found exactly this ordering bug in the first draft). |

"Cannot throw" is therefore a policy property of this function, not a style preference: a throw here is a silent allow. | Let it throw on a malformed rule (rejected — the failure mode is "the call goes through unexamined"). |
| 2026-08-21 | `match.when` ships in the type + evaluator even though NO seeded rule uses it. | Tension, flagged rather than silently resolved: AW-1 recommended shipping `match: { tool }` alone (YAGNI), but the TASK-224 card's acceptance criteria name "primitives-only predicates" explicitly and the plan's TDD code tests them. The card is the contract. AW-1's actual constraint — no seeded rule keys on tool input — is honoured. | Drop `when?` per AW-1 (rejected — fails a written acceptance criterion, and AW-4/AW-7 would re-add it). |
| 2026-08-21 | The plugin's cached capability rows are `Object.freeze`d. | The rows carry a security claim and are shared across every caller. The bus's `returns` zod re-parse already hands each caller a fresh object, so this is belt-and-braces against a future IN-PROCESS consumer (the package exports `capabilityRows` directly) editing a sentence in place and silently changing what every later reader is told the agent may do. | Rely on the zod re-parse (rejected — it protects the bus path only). |
| 2026-08-21 | The verdict-word check uses a per-word `\b…\b` regex, accepting that it over-rejects a legitimate hyphenated "first-class". | Space-padding let `never,` / `first-class` / `can/cannot` evade the gate entirely (see mistakes.md). On a claim about what an agent may do without asking, over-rejecting costs an author one reword; under-rejecting ships a sentence that contradicts the verdict it is filed under. Two tests pin BOTH directions — the four punctuation evasions, and that "candelabra"/"canvas" stay clean. | Enumerate punctuation in the padding (rejected — the next separator is always the one you forgot). Tokenize and set-test (equivalent; the regex reads better next to the other two checks). |
| 2026-08-21 | `rules.test.ts` asserts the seven named catalog facts are `provenance: 'catalog'` and that every rule declares provenance — NOT that `allow ⟹ catalog`. | The stricter form was wrong: a genuinely deliberated allow is legitimate, and it is the design's own §4.3.2 example ("Can reply to scheduling requests — on its own"). A test that rejects the spec's canonical example teaches the next author to weaken the test instead of thinking. | `allow ⟺ catalog` (rejected — forbids a shape the design shows). |

### AW-4 / TASK-225 — `@ax/decisions`, the row, the store, the pre-call gate (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | The Decision row's prose is **purely mechanical** — host-authored templates over `{capability, toolName}` in `templates.ts` — with NO per-rule template table. | The plan allowed "a per-rule authored template registered alongside the rule, else the mechanical fallback". `PolicyRule` carries no such fields and AW-4 does not modify `@ax/tool-policy`, so every rule falls to the fallback anyway. A per-`ruleId` table living inside `@ax/decisions` was rejected for a specific reason: invariant 2 forbids importing `BUILTIN_RULES`, so NOTHING could lint the two halves against each other, and a renamed rule would silently downgrade to the fallback — a drift with no detector. When a rule earns bespoke prose, the prose belongs on the rule. | A `ruleId → template` map in `@ax/decisions` (rejected — undetectable drift across a boundary). Add template fields to `PolicyRule` now (deferred — out of AW-4's file list, and no rule needs one yet). |
| 2026-08-21 | `kind`, `freshness` and `preview` are present in the row and the schema but **always `'action'` / `null` / `null`** in this PR. | Each would otherwise be invented. `kind: 'grant'` can only be inferred from a rule id (same drift hazard as above); a freshness predicate has no producer until AW-7, and claiming to have re-checked something is a promise the storage does not keep (H1); a `preview` synthesised out of `call.input` would put raw model output on a trust surface. Shipping the column and round-tripping it costs nothing and keeps AW-5/AW-7 additive. | Derive `kind` from the rule id (rejected). Omit the columns (rejected — a later migration for a field the design already names). |
| 2026-08-21 | The whole `tool:pre-call` subscriber body sits inside a catch that returns `reject(GATE_FAILURE_SENTENCE)`, and the outer wrapper ALSO rejects any non-`Rejection` return value. | `HookBus.fire` swallows a subscriber throw and continues, so for a subscriber whose only job is stopping tool calls a throw is a SILENT ALLOW — and a non-`undefined`, non-rejection return is worse: `fire` treats it as a MODIFIED PAYLOAD and would rewrite the tool call. Both failure modes are invisible. Six tests drive them (evaluate throws, store.create throws, malformed call, unknown verdict). | Let it throw and rely on the runner's fail-closed catch (rejected — the runner never sees a throw; `fire` ate it). |
| 2026-08-21 | `store.takeApproval` failing is NOT fatal — it logs and falls through to policy, which holds again. Every OTHER error rejects. | The two failures point opposite ways. "I could not check for an approval" degrades to asking again: annoying, safe. "I could not record this call" or "I could not get a verdict" must not let the call run. Failing closed uniformly would turn a transient DB blip into a denied turn where a second approval prompt was the honest answer. | Reject on every error (rejected — over-denies on the one path where re-asking is correct). |
| 2026-08-21 | The gate consumes a standing approval **before** calling `tool-policy:evaluate`, and a test asserts `evaluate` is never invoked on that path. | An approved call is never re-adjudicated: the human already decided, and a rule table edited between hold and approval would otherwise silently void an approval already given. Ordering is invisible in the happy path, so the test counts calls rather than checking the outcome. | Evaluate first and skip the hold if approved (rejected — lets policy overrule a human retroactively, with no trace). |
| 2026-08-21 | `decisions:undo` refuses once `consumedAt` is set. | Undo returns a row to `pending`, which correctly drops the standing authorisation (the partial unique index only covers `status='executed'`). But if the agent already consumed it, the call HAS run — and re-approving would authorise a SECOND execution of it. That bell cannot be un-rung, so the honest answer is `undone: false`. Enforced in the store's `restore` (a `consumed_at IS NULL` predicate), not only in the plugin. | Allow the undo and let AW-5 sort it out (rejected — a double-send is the exact failure the machine's rule 2 exists to prevent). |
| 2026-08-21 | `callFingerprint` is TOTAL: BigInt, cycles, functions and symbols all produce a digest instead of throwing, and its object-key filter matches exactly what `JSON.stringify` drops. | Two reasons, both load-bearing. (1) It runs inside the gate before anything can be vetoed, so a throw is a silent allow. (2) The call is persisted as JSON and read back — if the fingerprint of `{a: undefined}` disagreed with the fingerprint of `{}`, an approved call would stop matching ITSELF after a restart, and every approval would silently fail to authorise anything. Unserialisable inputs collapse to a name-only digest, which can only ever hold a call that might have passed — the safe direction. | Let it throw on exotic input (rejected — silent allow). Use `JSON.stringify` with a replacer (rejected — key order is not guaranteed, which is the whole point of the function). |
| 2026-08-21 | The k8s preset test asserts `@ax/decisions` is **LAST among the plugins that subscribe `tool:pre-call`**, computed from the manifests, rather than asserting a fixed index. | Registration order IS subscriber order, `fire` stops at the first rejection, and `Hold extends Rejection` — so a hold returned ahead of another subscriber's outright deny pre-empts it and asks a human to permit something the system already forbids. A fixed index rots the moment a plugin is inserted anywhere above; deriving the subscriber list from `manifest.subscribes` keeps the assertion true and load-bearing as the preset grows. The test also asserts `@ax/agent-activity` is in that list, so the check cannot pass vacuously with one subscriber. | Assert `indexOf(decisions) > indexOf(tool-policy)` alone (kept as a second assertion, but it does not cover a NEW denying subscriber added below). |
| 2026-08-21 | `@ax/tool-policy` was dropped alongside `@ax/decisions` in both preset acceptance canaries' `PLUGINS_TO_DROP`. | `@ax/decisions` is postgres-backed and those canaries swap postgres out, so it had to come off. But dropping it alone leaves `tool-policy:evaluate` with no caller and, worse, dropping ONLY tool-policy would leave the gate with no registrant — and the gate fails CLOSED, so every tool call in the canaries would come back denied. The pair goes together. | Stub `database:get-instance` for decisions in the canaries (rejected — the canaries deliberately run without postgres; stubbing it re-creates the coupling they exist to avoid). |

AW-12 adds the route and the control in one PR. | Register the 501 (rejected — Half-Wired Code Policy). |

Gating the route registration too is capability minimization (invariant 5) — with the flag off the surface does not exist server-side, not merely hidden client-side. | Authenticated flag route (rejected — the SPA wants it in the same `Promise.all` as the session, and the flag discloses nothing).
