### AW-5 / TASK-226 — Execute on approve: host replay, idempotency, expiry (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | `irreversible` is carried on `EvaluateResult` and **captured on the Decision row at hold time**, never re-read at approval time. | `PolicyRule.irreversible` existed but nothing could see it across the bus. Re-evaluating policy at approve time would second-guess a decision a human already made — and a rule edited between hold and approval would silently change what their click means. The policy that governs an approval is the policy that was in force when they were asked. | Re-call `tool-policy:evaluate` on approve (rejected — retroactively overrules a human, with no trace). A second `tool-policy:describe-rule` hook (rejected — same staleness, one more hook). |
| 2026-08-21 | A deferred (irreversible) replay is **durable** — `replay_due_at` plus a sweep that claims due rows with a conditional `UPDATE … SET replay_due_at = NULL … RETURNING` — not a `setTimeout`. | A timer dies with the process and is invisible to a second replica, so an approved send would either vanish on restart or happen twice under two hosts. Clearing the due-at inside the claiming UPDATE makes it one-shot across replicas. Accepted cost, documented in the store: a crash between claim and replay LOSES the replay — the row stays `executed` with no receipt, which reads as "approved, nothing happened". Wrong in the safe direction, versus a lease scheme that can double-send. | `setTimeout` per the plan's wording (rejected). A visible lease column + reaper (deferred — a follow-up card; not worth a second state machine for a 10-second window). |
| 2026-08-21 | `approved-pending-agent` is an **authorising** status: the partial unique index, `takeApproval` and `restore` all widen to `('executed','approved-pending-agent')`, driven off one exported `AUTHORISING_STATUSES`. | It is the status for a sandbox-only tool the host cannot replay, and its entire meaning is "the agent performs this on its next run". If the gate would not honour it, the status is a dead end and its receipt is a lie. Three hard-coded copies of that status list is how the three stop agreeing, so there is one. | Keep the row `executed` and add a separate boolean (rejected — `executed` is a claim the thing happened, design H1). |
| 2026-08-21 | `takeApproval` also refuses a row with a **pending deferred replay** (`replay_due_at IS NOT NULL`). | Without it, an agent that wakes inside the undo window consumes the authorisation, runs the call, and the sweep then replays it host-side too. One approval, two sends — the exact failure the whole file exists to prevent. | Rely on the agent not being warm on the unattended path (rejected — "unattended" is about the conversation, not a guarantee the agent never runs again). |
| 2026-08-21 | The approve path **claims first, then acts** — `claimForApproval` is a conditional `UPDATE … WHERE status IN ('pending','stale')`, and the replay runs only for the caller that won it. | Acting first and recording afterwards leaves, on a crash in between, an action that happened behind a row that says it did not — and the human's next click does it twice. A `null` from the claim means SOMEONE ELSE RESOLVED IT, not "no such row"; every such branch re-reads and reports the stored outcome. | Replay then mark (rejected). Application-level mutex (rejected — does not survive two replicas). |
| 2026-08-21 | A unique-index violation from `claimForApproval` is **absorbed**, logged at `warn`, and reported as the stored outcome — not surfaced as an internal error. | Reachable without any bug: the agent holds the same call twice, a human approves both rows. The second claim hits the partial unique index. The call is already authorised; nothing about that is a 500. Follow-up card filed for collapsing duplicate holds at the gate. | Let it throw (rejected — a plain user action becomes an error page). |
| 2026-08-21 | The attended path fires **no** `decisions:executed` receipt. | The host ran nothing; AW-6 owns delivery to the warm agent. A receipt for something that has not happened is design H1 in one line. Undo therefore only retracts a receipt for a row that had one (`executed` / `approved-pending-agent`). | Fire an `approved` receipt on every path (rejected). |
| 2026-08-21 | Four authored receipt strings, none derived from another: `approvedText` (executed), `FAILED_RECEIPT`, `PENDING_AGENT_RECEIPT`, `RETRACTED_RECEIPT`; a test asserts no pairwise containment. | Same trap as `approvedText`/`dismissedText`. The failure line especially must not be reachable from the approved one by string surgery, because the approved one claims the thing happened. `PENDING_AGENT_RECEIPT` is the card's exact sentence and never says "Sent". | Template the failure line off the approved one (rejected — that is literally the bug design H1 names). |
| 2026-08-21 | The host executor's error message is **sanitised** (`sanitizeFailureDetail`: control chars stripped, clamped 200) before it is stored or crosses the bus, and it is never the receipt. | A host tool's message can quote model-authored input back at us, and `replay_error` reaches a renderer. Stripping CR/LF stops a crafted message forging a separate line; keeping the receipt authored stops it becoming the sentence a human reads as a factual claim. | Store the raw message (rejected — untrusted content on a trust surface). |
| 2026-08-21 | A successful host replay stamps a **separate `replayed_at`** column, and that column is a predicate on the partial unique index, on `takeApproval` and on `restore`. | Found while reviewing: without it, a row the host had already run stayed `executed` with `consumed_at` null, so (a) the agent's next byte-identical call cashed in a yes the host had already spent, (b) an undo put the row back on the queue for a second run, and (c) a later hold of the same call could never be approved — the old row still occupied the index slot. `consumed_at` stays what its docstring says (the AGENT took it up); who ran it is a different fact and gets its own field. | Reuse `consumed_at` for the host replay (rejected — conflates two actors, and the plan's canary explicitly asserts `consumedAt` is unset after a replay). Do nothing (rejected — one approval, two executions). |
| 2026-08-21 | A fifth column, `replay_claimed_at`, marks the replay **in flight** — set in the same statement that claims it, never cleared — and is a predicate on `takeApproval` and `restore`. | Reviewer-caught blocker. `replayed_at` closes the door only AFTER the executor returns; between the host committing to the call and the call returning, the row is `executed` with nothing consumed, so a byte-identical agent call landing in that window spent the same yes and ran the call a second time. Milliseconds wide, but reachable across replicas and completely untested. It also makes the deferred sweep's claim genuinely one-shot: setting the stamp and clearing `replay_due_at` in one UPDATE means a second sweep matches nothing, where clearing alone re-opened the row to the agent for the whole flight. Canary test vacuity-checked by removing the predicate and watching it go red. | Reuse `replay_due_at` as the in-flight marker (rejected — the sweep would then re-claim it). Accept the window as too narrow to matter (rejected — "narrow" is not a property you get to keep once there are two replicas). |
| 2026-08-21 | `parkForAgent` **clears** `replay_claimed_at` as well as `replay_due_at`. | Second reviewer catch. That method is only ever reached from inside `settleReplay`, i.e. on a row the host had already claimed, so leaving the in-flight marker set parked a decision the agent was then forbidden to consume — the call would have run ZERO times, a silent strand. Parking means the host handed the flight back without sending, so the marker must drop with it. The existing tests missed it because they parked a row with `replayClaimedAt: null`, a precondition that never occurs in production. | Leave it set (rejected — inaction is still the failure this package exists to prevent). |
| 2026-08-21 | Undo is **refused** once the host replay has completed, and the `retracted` receipt therefore fires only for states where nothing has run yet (`approved-pending-agent`, an unconsumed attended `executed`, a deferred replay inside its window). | A deliberate, narrow deviation from the card's literal wording ("undo of an executed decision fires retracted"). Allowing it after the call was made would let a re-approval run the call a second time, and would remove a receipt for something that genuinely happened — a lie in the other direction. It is the same rule TASK-225 already wrote for `consumed_at`; the plan's own "undo does not un-send an email" is the argument for it. | Allow the undo and re-run on re-approval (rejected — double execution). Allow the undo and block re-approval (rejected — a decision stuck in `pending` that no button can resolve). |
| 2026-08-21 | The replay's `AgentContext` is built from the DECISION's `(ownerUserId, agentId, conversationId)` and sets `workspace.rootPath` EXPLICITLY to `process.cwd()`. | Firing with the approving request's ctx would route downstream `workspace:*` work by the wrong `(userId, agentId)` — the repo has been bitten by exactly that on `workspace:apply`. There is no session workspace to inherit here because the turn ended, so the host cwd is stated rather than defaulted, which is also what host-side plugins already see on host-initiated paths. | Reuse the approver's ctx (rejected — wrong workspace, and the approver need not be the owner in a future shared-agent world). |

### AW-10 / TASK-231 — one Activity feed over one collection (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | The feed got its OWN route, `GET /api/workspace/activity`, and `activity` was **removed** from `GET /api/workspace/state` rather than being filled in. | Two things forced it. (1) Acceptance requires pagination on `before: <ISO firedAt>`, and a sub-array of a state blob cannot be paginated — a "load more" would have to re-fetch the whole roster response. (2) `/state` already fans out one `conversations:list` per agent for the liveness probe (AW-9); adding a second per-agent fan-out there doubles the cost of the page everyone lands on. Keeping BOTH a `/state.activity` and the route would have been invariant 4 violated in the BFF — the exact thing this card exists to remove — so the field is gone and the collection has one producer. | Fill `/state.activity` from the same reads (rejected — unpaginable, second N+1 on the hot path). Keep `/state.activity` as the first page and the route for subsequent ones (rejected — two producers, and they drift the moment one grows a filter). |
| 2026-08-21 | `nextBefore` is the instant of the last fire **CONSIDERED**, not of the last event **RENDERED**, and the server supplies it rather than the client deriving it. | A `silenced` fire renders as nothing (H1), so a page of fires can legitimately produce ZERO events with more history behind it. A client paginating on its last visible row would have no cursor at all on a quiet stretch and the feed would dead-end — silently, looking exactly like "that's everything". The distinction is invisible until a real deployment has a silenced routine, which is most of them. | Client paginates on the last rendered `at` (rejected — dead-ends on an all-silenced page). Return a row count and paginate by offset (rejected — offsets skip rows when new fires land above). |
| 2026-08-21 | `ActivityEvent.id` is the composite `` `${agentId}|${path}|${iso}` ``, not `FireRow.id`. | `FireRow.id` is a `BIGSERIAL` — storage vocabulary that leaked into a hook payload before this card existed. The card scopes out fixing it, but it must not reach the wire, and a React key IS the wire. The composite is stable across pages and reproducible on any backend. Cost: two fires of one routine in the same millisecond would collide; fires are seconds-apart tick events, so that is not a case we have. | Use the row id as the key (rejected — puts the leak on the wire). Use the array index (rejected — unstable across appended pages, which is exactly when React needs it stable). |
| 2026-08-21 | `ActivityEvent` **dropped** `day` and `time` for a single ISO `at`; the client buckets by LOCAL date and formats its own clock. | The prototype computed both server-side. Every reader outside the server's timezone got rows filed under the wrong day and a clock that disagreed with their own — and it fails silently, because the string always LOOKS right. A rendering decision does not belong on the wire. Knock-on: "Today" now stays true across midnight without a refetch, since it is recomputed against `new Date()` at render. | Send an offset alongside the strings (rejected — the server still picks the day, it is just wrong more subtly). Send both and let the client prefer `at` (rejected — two sources for one fact). |
| 2026-08-21 | The scoped read (`?agentId=`) is **strict** — a failure propagates; the unscoped roster fan-out is **non-strict** — a failing agent is logged and skipped. | Same split `listConversations` already makes, for the same reason. On one agent's "What it did" tab that history IS the page, so a swallowed read would render "nothing recorded yet" over a failure nobody was told about (H7). On the roster-wide page, failing the whole feed because one agent hiccuped trades a small wrong for a big one. | Strict everywhere (rejected — one bad agent 500s the Activity page). Non-strict everywhere (rejected — turns a failure into a claim on the tab where the claim is loudest). |
| 2026-08-21 | `routines:list` is ALWAYS called per-agent, never once unscoped, even though the unscoped call would save N-1 round trips on the global feed. | `routines:list` with no `agentId` returns **every** routine in the deployment, including other users'. The only thing this call supplies is a `path → authored name` map for labelling; buying that with a cross-tenant read is not a trade. A failed name read degrades to labelling rows with their path — a worse label, never a wrong one, and never a dropped row. | One unscoped call plus a client-side filter (rejected — the leak already happened server-side by then). Cache a global map at boot (rejected — same leak, plus staleness). |
| 2026-08-21 | Both routines hooks are declared `optionalCall`s, and an absent `routines:recent-fires-for-agent` returns `{events: [], nextBefore: null}` rather than an error. | A deployment without `@ax/routines` records no routine history at all, so empty is the TRUE answer, not a swallowed read — this is the one place on this surface where an empty array is not a claim. Distinguished in the code from the failure path, which logs and (when scoped) throws. | Hard-declare the calls (rejected — channel-web loads in presets that have no routines). Return 503 when absent (rejected — reports a fault where there is none). |
| 2026-08-21 | Today's "Done" filter needed no removal — AW-9 already cut it — so this card's share of that acceptance line was the missing half: a real `doneToday` count in the digest sub-line. | The sub-line and its "Everything they did" link shipped with AW-9, but with nothing behind them; the reassurance the Done filter used to carry had no producer until the feed became real. The count obeys the file's existing commented rule — rendered only when positive, because a zero next to a green tick reads as a report on a system nobody measured. | Leave the sub-line as-is and call the line satisfied (rejected — the reassurance the design moved there would still be absent). Add a "0 done today" row (rejected — the exact zero-as-claim bug that file documents). |
| 2026-08-21 | The decision-receipt half (AW-10 step 5, `decisions:executed`) was **not stubbed** — it is a follow-up. | `@ax/decisions` on main registers only list/get/approve/dismiss/undo; the hook does not exist, and the card says explicitly to ship without it rather than stub. A subscription to a hook nobody fires is half-wired code that reads as a working feature. | Subscribe defensively behind `hasService` (rejected — Half-Wired Code Policy; nothing would ever fire it). |

### AW-13 / TASK-234 — a human-owned memory tier the rollup may not touch (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | The exclusion is a RUNTIME GUARD plus a STATIC CANARY, not a comment and not a per-writer assertion. `human-tier.ts` exports `AUTOMATIC_WRITERS` (one entry per mutating module, `excludes` being the shared `HUMAN_TIER_PATHS` array itself, not a copy) and `guardAutomaticWrite(writer, path)`, which every write/unlink site calls. `human-tier.test.ts` scans `packages/memory-strata/src/**` for FS-mutation calls and fails when a module performs one without being registered. | The failure this card exists to prevent is a writer added in six months by someone who never read the comment. A per-writer test ("the rollup does not touch rules.md") only covers the writers that exist today. Mutation-tested: removing `map.ts` from the list turns the canary red. | A comment (rejected — the plan says so explicitly). A path allow-list checked only inside `flushAgentTier` (rejected — misses the CLI preset, which writes the host FS directly). |
| 2026-08-21 | `flushAgentTier` FILTERS the human tier out of its computed delta (`stripHumanTierChanges`) rather than throwing, and every other site throws. | The flush's delta is DERIVED from a whole-subtree diff, not authored: a scratch hydrated before a concurrent human write yields a spurious `delete` for a file the pipeline never touched. Throwing there would fail an otherwise-correct consolidation over a race. Everywhere else, a writer aimed at `rules.md` is a bug and must be loud. | Throw in the flush too (rejected — turns a benign race into a failed pass). Filter everywhere (rejected — hides real bugs). |
| 2026-08-21 | `inject.ts` reads the human tier through `readRules()` (raw), NOT through `readSystemBody`/`readTierSystemBody`. | Those strip a leading `---` fence as YAML frontmatter. Every machine-written system file carries one; the human tier deliberately carries none, so a user whose first line is a markdown horizontal rule would watch the top of their own rules vanish. Verbatim has to mean verbatim, or the tier's promise is broken by its own reader. | Add `'rules'` to `InjectedSystemName` as the plan literally said (rejected — inherits the frontmatter strip). |
| 2026-08-21 | The human tier is rendered FIRST in the injected block and truncated LAST (a new step 5 after User Profile in `assembleUnderCap`). | Position is precedence, and the drop order is the budget's opinion about whose words matter. Every section the agent wrote for itself yields before one word the user typed does. | Leave rules in the existing step-4 tier (rejected — a long map could evict a user's rule). |
| 2026-08-21 | `bootstrap.ts` does not seed `rules.md`, and cannot: `SeededSystemFileName = Exclude<SystemFileName, 'rules'>` plus the absence of a `system/rules` member in `MemoryFileType` make it a compile error. | An absent rules file and an empty one mean the same thing to every reader, so seeding buys nothing — and bootstrap is an automatic writer. Making it a type error rather than a missing entry in a literal means widening the loop fails the build, not a user. | Seed an empty file with `wx` (rejected — harmless today, but it puts an automatic writer on the path by convention only). |
| 2026-08-21 | Three hooks, not two: `memory:rules:read` / `memory:rules:write` (as planned) plus `memory:learned:read`. | The design says the agent's own notes are "inspectable", and a permanently empty "What it worked out" section reads as broken on a tab whose entire subject is honesty. `memory:learned:read` returns the same three always-injected docs `inject.ts` builds the prompt from, so the tab shows what the agent actually reads. | Ship the section empty until a later card (rejected — a labelled heading over nothing, on this tab of all tabs). Reuse `memory:index:search` (rejected — a search is not "what is always in your context"). |
| 2026-08-21 | Every hook takes `agentId` in the payload even though `ctx` carries one, and rejects a mismatch. | `workspace:apply` routes by `(userId, agentId)` off the ctx. The established regression is a caller firing with someone else's ctx and landing the write in the wrong workspace — silently. Carrying the id the caller BELIEVES it is writing turns that into a loud `invalid-payload`. The channel-web route builds its own owner-routed ctx from the authenticated user and asserts on it in a test. | Trust the ctx alone (rejected — the wrong-ctx bug is exactly the one that has shipped before, and it is undetectable from inside the hook). |
| 2026-08-21 | `PUT /api/workspace/agents/:agentId/memory/rules` answers **503 `memory-unavailable`** when no memory plugin is loaded, and the three hooks are NOT in `channel-web`'s `manifest.calls`. | memory-strata is optional in both presets (CLI `--memory`, k8s `cfg.hostLlmTools`). Declaring the calls would make the kernel's `verifyCalls` refuse to boot a deployment that simply chose not to run memory. Answering 200 would tell a user their rules were kept when nothing kept them — the exact lie the tier exists to stop. | Declare them hard (rejected — breaks memory-less deployments). Return 200 and drop the text (rejected — silent failure). |
### AW-6 / TASK-227 — Attendance and the `decision-resolved` delivery (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | Attendance is read through **`conversations:get-metadata`**, not `conversations:get` as the plan said — and that hook was widened with `origin` + `activeSessionId` so the attendance lookup and the delivery lookup are the SAME single indexed row read. | `conversations:get` calls `store.listEvents()` and reconstructs attachment blocks: its cost grows with the conversation. The attendance read rides inside the `tool:pre-call` 10 s ceiling, and a gate that gets slower as a thread gets longer is a gate that eventually denies. The plan's own words were "a single indexed read and nothing more". `origin` is still on the `Conversation` domain type, so `conversations:get` carries it too. | Use `conversations:get` per the plan's letter (rejected — display-event scan on the gate's budget). A third read hook (rejected — `get-metadata` already IS the cheap projection). |
| 2026-08-21 | Both new hook dependencies are **`optionalCalls`, not `calls`**: `conversations:get-metadata` (degrade → everything unattended) and `session:queue-work` (degrade → no delivery; the standing authorisation reaches the agent's next run). | A required `call` fails the BOOT when its producer is absent. `@ax/decisions` runs perfectly well in a host with neither — the degradations are both the fail-safe direction, and a headless deployment genuinely wants "always unattended". `preset.test.ts` then has to assert the k8s preset DOES load both producers, because an `optionalCall` silently degrading is exactly what nothing else would catch. | Hard `calls` (rejected — unloadable in its own canary preset). No manifest entry at all (rejected — an undeclared cross-plugin dependency). |
| 2026-08-21 | `attendanceFor` **fails to `unattended`** on every unknown: no conversation id, an unreadable row, a foreign row, an `origin` value this build does not recognise, no conversations store at all. | The two mistakes are not symmetric. Unattended misread as attended strands the decision waiting for a warm agent that is already gone — nothing runs, ever, and nothing says so. Attended misread as unattended just means the host replays the recorded call itself; it still happens, the agent merely does not get to narrate it. | Default to `attended` (rejected — the silent-strand direction). Keep AW-4's `ctx.source` guess as the fallback (rejected — it answers a different question and would make the fallback disagree with the primary path). |
| 2026-08-21 | `defaultAttendanceFor` (AW-4's `ctx.source === 'routine'` stub) was **deleted**, and `PreCallDeps.attendanceFor` became REQUIRED and async. | `ctx.source` answers "was this a scheduled fire", which is a different question that happens to have the same answer only while `packages/` holds exactly two channels. Leaving it as a default meant a caller that forgot to supply a resolver got a plausible-looking guess instead of a compile error. The canary's `routineCtx` deliberately no longer sets `source: 'routine'` — if anything in the gate starts reading it again, that is where it would otherwise hide. | Keep it as the fallback (rejected — two disagreeing definitions of attendance). |
| 2026-08-21 | `inbox-loop.ts`'s terminal `throw` on an unrecognised `session.next-message` type became **log-and-re-poll**, advancing the cursor only FORWARD. | BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, flagged in the PR. The throw was defensible while the union was closed; it stopped being defensible the moment the union started growing, because a host newer than a runner now legitimately delivers variants that runner predates — and the old behaviour turned a forward-compatible addition into a crashed turn on every unrebuilt runner in the fleet. The forward-only cursor guard matters: skipping an entry we cannot act on is fine, REPLAYING one we already delivered would answer a user message twice. | Keep the throw (rejected — kills healthy turns on version skew). Advance the cursor unconditionally (rejected — a bogus cursor rewinds into delivered entries). |
| 2026-08-21 | `fetchEntry` in `@ax/session-postgres` now **throws `corrupt-inbox-row`** for an unknown row `type`, where it used to `return null`. | Found while adding the fourth entry type. A null at a cursor that HAS a row makes the claim loop re-poll forever — the runner hangs with no diagnostic, which is the exact scenario the user-message branch's corruption throw was written to prevent. The trailing `return null` was that same hazard hiding one branch away. | Leave the fallthrough (rejected — silent hang). |
| 2026-08-21 | The delivery handles the entry in **`agent-runner-core/run-runner.ts`'s `nextMessage()`**, one implementation, not in both runner shells as the plan listed. | `nextMessage` is already shared: both `@ax/agent-claude-sdk-runner` and `@ax/agent-aisdk-runner` call `runRunner`, and the message pump lives in the core. Two copies of the branch would be two places to forget. | Duplicate it per the plan's file list (rejected). |
| 2026-08-21 | A host-initiated turn **clears `currentReqId`** rather than inheriting the previous turn's. | No `agent:invoke` is in flight, so no client is waiting. An unset reqId makes the shell skip the `event.stream-chunk` emission outright; a STALE one asks the host to route chunks at a request that already completed. The turn's content still reaches the user through `event.turn-end` → the display event log. Live streaming of a host-initiated turn is AW-11's problem. | Keep the last reqId (rejected — stale correlation). |
| 2026-08-21 | The card's "an attended decision whose session is gone **stays in the queue**" is asserted as *the standing authorisation survives and the agent's next call consumes it exactly once* — NOT as `status === 'pending'`. | The plan's literal test contradicts AW-5: `claimForApproval` already moved the row out of `pending` in the same write that won the claim, so `decisions:list({status:'pending'})` can never contain it. Re-opening a decision a person has already answered would be a lie about what they did. What the design actually claims (§3.3, "no special case is written anywhere") is that the attended path degrades INTO the unattended one — and that is what the authorisation surviving means. | Assert `status: 'pending'` as written (rejected — it cannot pass, and making it pass would mean un-answering a human's click). |
| 2026-08-21 | A one-shot **backfill** sets `origin = 'routine'` where `origin IS NULL AND hidden = TRUE`. | The rest of the column takes no backfill, correctly — NULL reads as `'web'` and an existing conversation is by definition one a human opened. But that reads a ROUTINE's pre-existing conversation as attended, the wrong direction. A per-fire row ages out; a `conversation: shared` routine keeps ONE row forever, so it would be misclassified for good. `hidden = TRUE` is the honest key: every writer of it is the routines path (`create`/`find-or-create` with `hidden: true`, and `conversations:hide`, whose only caller is the routines silence-token logic). | No backfill at all per the card (rejected — permanent misclassification of shared routine conversations, in the silent-strand direction). Backfill on `external_key IS NOT NULL` (rejected — misses per-fire rows). |
| 2026-08-21 | A dismissal is delivered too, and **gated on `saved !== null`** — the caller that actually won the conditional `markDismissed` update. | An attended agent is parked on its inbox waiting for the answer; without the dismissal it sits there until the idle floor expires and then dies mid-thought, never learning the call was turned down. Gating on the winner stops a second tab's click waking the agent again with news it already has. | Deliver on approve only (rejected — the agent is parked either way). Deliver unconditionally (rejected — duplicate wake). |

### AW-11 / TASK-232 — the Today queue on real decisions (2026-08-21)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-21 | The browser's `Decision` is a **PROJECTION** of `@ax/decisions`' row, not a copy. Dropped on the wire: `call` (input and all), `ownerUserId`, `callFingerprint`, `ruleId`, `consumedAt`, `replayClaimedAt`, `replayedAt`, `replayError`. Added: `pendingUntil` (renderer-facing name for `replayDueAt`) and `undoable` (server-derived). | Capability minimisation applies to a wire shape exactly as it does to a filesystem path (invariant 5). `call.input` is model-authored, nothing renders it, and shipping it would put raw model output on a trust surface (design H6) — the SSE frame drops it for the same reason and now so does the REST payload, which makes "the input never reaches the client" true by construction rather than by renderer discipline. The four replay-bookkeeping fields answer exactly one question a renderer has — can this still be taken back — so the server answers that question instead of shipping the four fields and letting the client re-derive it, which is how a second copy of the decision machine gets built by accident. | Re-export the plugin's full row (rejected — cross-plugin import, plus every field above on the wire). Ship the row and let renderers ignore what they do not need (rejected — "the renderer does not read it" is not a security property). |
| 2026-08-21 | `/api/workspace/state` **drops** `decisions` entirely; `GET /api/workspace/decisions` is the sole producer. | Identical reasoning to AW-10 moving `activity` off `/state`: two fields over one collection is invariant 4 violated in the BFF, and `/state`'s per-agent liveness probe is already an N+1 that a second fan-out would double. It also gives the three writes somewhere to live next to the read whose rows they change. | Keep `decisions` on `/state` and add the POST routes only (rejected — two producers; the queue would then have a read that the writes could not update). |
| 2026-08-21 | **No optimistic status transition on the client at all.** A click marks its row BUSY (controls disabled, "Working on it…"), and the server's returned row is what lands. | To pick a status to flip TO, the client would have to know which of five outcomes an approval takes — executed, approved-pending-agent, deferred, stale, or absorbed-because-expired — which IS the machine, rebuilt on the client and wrong for three of them. A row that briefly reads "Sent" and then corrects itself to "it will do this the next time it runs" has already told someone something untrue (H1). A failed POST therefore has nothing to roll back; it leaves the row untouched and posts a notice on it. | Optimistically mark `executed` and reconcile (rejected — that is the client-side machine invariant 4 forbids, and it lies for three of five outcomes). No busy state at all (rejected — a click with no feedback reads as a swallowed click). |
| 2026-08-21 | The undo affordance is gated on **two** things — the server's `undoable` AND the ten-second clock from `resolvedAt` — and `undoable` is the one that matters. | The card's acceptance names the clock, but the clock is not the dangerous case: a reversible call the host replays IMMEDIATELY is `executed` with `replayedAt` set within milliseconds, still deep inside the ten seconds, and `decisions:undo` refuses it. A clock-only gate would have shown "Undo · 9s" on an email that had already gone, and clicking it would have done nothing. The server already knows; it now says so in one boolean. The client still keeps the clock so the button disappears on time rather than on the next fetch. | Clock only (rejected — a live dead button on a sent action, the exact control the card calls the worst on this surface). Server flag only (rejected — the button would linger until the next poll). |
| 2026-08-21 | Every prose field on a decision is **fenced server-side** in the projection — summary, detail, staleReason, the three labels, both receipt lines, `freshness.label`, and both preview halves — with the same `fenceLine` the activity feed uses, and the labels fall back to fixed constants when they fence to nothing. | The strings are host-authored but built from tool names and capability clauses that arrive from MCP servers and agent-authored skills, so this route is the trust boundary. Bidi overrides are the live risk (CVE-2021-42574 pointed at an approval card: a `‮` in a summary reorders everything after it, including the row's own timestamp). A label fenced to nothing must NOT render as a blank button — an unnamed control on an approval surface is worse than a generic one, so `Approve` / `Open the conversation` / `Dismiss` are the floor. | Fence in the renderer (rejected — bounds what one component draws, not what goes on the wire, and the SSE frame has no renderer to fence in). Trust the strings because we authored the template (rejected — the template's slots are not ours). |
| 2026-08-21 | The in-thread `ApprovalCard` **drops the secondary button** and renders `detail` inline instead. | `secondaryLabel` is "Show me the details"; in the queue it opens the agent, and from inside the agent's own thread there is nowhere for it to go. The version this replaced wired it to DISMISS — so a person asking to see more would have turned the request down. A control that does something other than what it says is worse than no control. | Wire it to a no-op (rejected — swallowed click). Keep it wired to dismiss (rejected — actively harmful). |
| 2026-08-21 | The JIT permission card does **not** converge onto `Decision`, and the reasoning is written into `PermissionCard.tsx`'s header rather than only into a PR description. | A JIT card is a durable capability GRANT with no recorded call to replay and no outcome to report; a Decision is a one-shot outward ACTION with a verbatim call and a freshness guard. Collapsing them forces null `call`, null `freshness`, a meaningless `approvedText`, and a resolution path (`regenerate()`) sharing no code with the host replay. `kind: 'grant'` stays on `Decision` because a grant raised THROUGH a hold is a real case — the JIT card is not that case. In the file, because the question comes up every time someone reads both surfaces. | Merge them behind one component (rejected — three lies and a switch statement in exchange for one component). |
| 2026-08-21 | `decisionRaised` is consumed by the workspace's own SSE reader and triggers a **re-read**, not a render. | The frame carries an id and a summary only, so there is nothing to draw from it — and drawing from it would create a second description of a row we already have a producer for. Re-reading brings back the thread with its approval message and the decision into the same array Today renders, so the card in the thread and the row in the queue are literally the same object. Without this consumer the frame would have been half-wired: a server push nothing listened to. | Render the summary straight off the frame (rejected — second source of truth for one row, and a card whose buttons act on a row we never fetched). Leave the frame unconsumed for a later card (rejected — Half-Wired Code Policy). |
### AW-12 / TASK-233 — the Files and What-it-did tabs (2026-08-22)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-22 | The Files tab is its OWN route pair (`GET .../files`, `GET .../files/*`), and `files` is REMOVED from `AgentDetail`. | Same reason the activity feed left `/state` in AW-10: a sub-array inside a 200 cannot carry the difference between "this agent has written nothing" and "we could not read its workspace", and the prototype rendered the second as the first. A dedicated route can answer 503, 500 or an honest empty, and the tab has four distinct sentences for the four cases. | Fill `AgentDetail.files` from the listing (rejected — reintroduces the exact ambiguity, and makes the detail read pay for a workspace listing on every tab). |

The sanitizer alone is wrong for a READER (it would serve `_/_/etc/passwd` for `../../etc/passwd`), so the port supplies the containment logic and the verdict — output != input means 400 — is ours. `assertWithinBase` was deliberately NOT ported: nothing here reads a path back out of storage, and an uncalled function is half-wired code. | Re-derive a bespoke validator (rejected — the card forbids it). Port both helpers (rejected — half-wired). |

Excluding only the plan's spelling would have excluded nothing where it matters and put the human-owned rules file on a tab with different editing rules. Both are listed. One predicate because an exclusion the listing enforces and the read does not is a cosmetic filter with a direct-URL bypass behind it. | Push it into `workspace:list`'s `pathGlob` (rejected — the two backends in this repo do not agree on glob syntax, and it would put "what we serve" in two spellings). |
| 2026-08-22 | No `pathGlob` at all: the BFF lists everything and filters in process, capped at 500 rows with `truncated` on the wire. | Same one-predicate argument, plus `pathGlob` is advisory (memory-strata already re-filters defensively after calling it). The cap is a bound on somebody else's output; announcing it is what stops a short list from reading as a complete one. | Trust the backend glob (rejected — advisory). Return everything (rejected — unbounded response built from agent-controlled data). |
| 2026-08-22 | The listing is STRICT (a `workspace:list` throw propagates) and answers **503 `workspace-unavailable`** when no backend is registered. | TASK-231's split, applied here: on this tab the listing IS the page, so a swallowed failure renders "has not written anything yet" over a workspace nobody looked at (H7). 503 is separate from 500 because "this deployment runs no workspace backend" is not a blip — the UI drops the Try-again button for it, since retrying will never change the answer. | Degrade to `[]` like the roster fan-out (rejected — the fan-out has other rows to show; this tab has none). |
| 2026-08-22 | `workspace:list` is declared a HARD `call` in channel-web's manifest, unlike the memory hooks. | `workspace:read` and `workspace:apply` are already hard there on the argument that every preset loading channel-web loads a workspace backend, and all four base workspace hooks are registered by the same plugin — so `workspace:list` cannot be absent where `workspace:read` is present. That is exactly the opposite of memory-strata, which is genuinely optional in both presets (decision 2026-08-21). The 503 branch stays anyway; it costs three lines and covers a harness that registers one hook and not the other. | Optional call (rejected — misrepresents a hook that ships in the same bundle as one already declared hard). |
| 2026-08-22 | `react-markdown` becomes a DIRECT dependency of `@ax/channel-web`, and the URL policy moves into a new `components/Markdown.tsx` that `MarkdownText` imports. | The plan says "render through the markdown pipeline the package already uses; do not add a second one" — but that pipeline is `MarkdownTextPrimitive`, which reads its text from `useMessagePartText()` and cannot render a string. `react-markdown` IS what the primitive runs internally, at the version already resolved in the lockfile, so calling it directly with the SAME shared `safeUrlTransform` is one pipeline used twice. It also deletes a wart: `MarkdownText` carried an inlined copy of react-markdown's `safeProtocol` regex under a comment apologising for not being able to import it. Lockfile delta is three lines (an importer entry against the existing resolution), no new transitive surface. | Stand up an assistant-ui runtime around a file viewer (rejected — absurd, and pulls the thread runtime into a surface that deliberately does not mount it). Raw HTML was already inert (no `rehype-raw`), and `javascript:`/`data:` are already blanked by the shared transform. | Reuse `MarkdownText`'s component table wholesale (rejected — inherits the artifact-chip widening and remote images on the one surface that should have neither). |

A Files tab shows whatever the agent wrote, which is mostly not markdown. | Render every body as markdown (rejected — silently corrupts the majority case). |
| 2026-08-22 | "What it did" needed NO component change — it was already `<ActivityFeed agentId={agent.id} />` over `useActivityFeed(route.id)` from AW-10. Two regression tests were added instead. | The plan's own step 4 says that if this tab needs more than passing the prop, the AW-10 component is not one component and THAT is the bug. It did not. What was missing was the guard: nothing asserted the shell scopes the FETCH to the open agent, so an unscoped feed under one agent's heading would have been a 200 that quietly means something else and looks completely normal. Now pinned on both sides — scoped when an agent is open, unscoped on the Activity page. | Leave it untested because it already worked (rejected — the failure mode is invisible). |

### TASK-259 — Undo stays on screen after the call already ran (2026-08-22)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-22 | The fix is a bounded POLL of one row, not an SSE push, and it needs a new `GET /api/workspace/decisions/:decisionId`. | The server was already right — `undoable` goes false the instant `consumedAt` or `replayedAt` is set. The client simply never heard it: it applied the approve response (always `undoable: true`, captured a millisecond after `resolvedAt`) and never read the row again, which made `undoSecondsLeft`'s first gate unreachable. A full `refresh()` cannot fix that: `decisions:list` defaults to the OPEN statuses, so re-reading the queue would DROP the just-resolved receipt row — the very row carrying the Undo. The re-read has to be per-row. | SSE `decisions:executed` (rejected for now — a new subscriber hook + a per-user SSE endpoint + a client transport the workspace surface does not have yet, all to shave <1s off a 10s window; the card offered either). Poll the list route (rejected — returns open rows only, would delete the receipt). |
| 2026-08-22 | A polled row may only overwrite a row that is STILL inside its own undo window (`applyPolledRow`'s guard), and rows with a POST in flight are not polled at all. | This is the race: a poll already in flight when the person clicks Undo lands AFTER the undo's own response, and without the guard it puts the just-approved row back on screen — the click visibly un-happens. Doing it inside the functional `setDecisions` updater makes the check atomic with the write, so no ref-sync bug can reopen it. | Drop stale responses by comparing timestamps (rejected — a second clock to disagree with). Cancel in-flight polls on click (rejected — AbortController plumbing for a case the guard already closes). |
| 2026-08-22 | A FAILED poll changes nothing, shows no notice, and does not hide the affordance. | Three reasons. It is never worse than today — before this change the client was permanently in the failed-poll state. Undo stays honest at click time: the server refuses a late one and the row says "That had already happened, so it could not be taken back". And hiding a working safety net on a network blip is the more harmful error of the two: the person then cannot stop something they still could have stopped. At 1s cadence it takes ~10 consecutive failures to lose a whole window. | Show a notice (rejected — nobody clicked anything, so nobody is owed an answer; a blip is not news). Hide Undo on poll failure (rejected — removes a real safety net on transient noise). |

### TASK-254 — collapse a duplicate pending hold at the gate (2026-08-23)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-23 | The gate **REUSES the open row** — `store.createOrReuseOpen(decision)` returns `{decision, created}`, and on `created:false` the hold points at the standing row and the minted row is never written. No second unique index. | The property to preserve is "the human is never asked the same question twice for one call, and approving what they are shown authorises it exactly once". Reuse delivers both directly. The index alternative delivers neither on its own: a refusal at the gate has to degrade into something, and the something would be a hold that fails to raise. Worse, the index would bind `restore` too — undo moves rows INTO `pending`, and dismiss → agent retries → undo (or deferred approval → agent retries → undo) reaches that with an identical open row present, turning `decisions:undo` into a 500. Pinned by a store test that performs exactly that sequence and asserts the undo still works. | A partial unique index over the open statuses (rejected — see above). Leaving it to `claimForApproval` to report (rejected — that is TASK-253's half, and it does not stop the person being asked twice). |
| 2026-08-23 | Atomicity comes from a **transaction-scoped advisory lock** (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`) keyed on a sha256 of `(agentId, callFingerprint)` truncated to a signed int64, taken inside the same transaction as the SELECT + INSERT. | The caller's read-then-create is a TOCTOU and two byte-identical `tool:pre-call` events genuinely race. Watched failing 8 rows out of 8 with a warm pool before the lock existed. Transaction-scoped so it cannot be leaked by a caller that forgets to unlock; keyed per (agent, call) so unrelated holds never queue behind each other; the key derived in JS rather than via `hashtext()` because that is an undocumented Postgres internal and two replicas mid-upgrade must agree on the key or they are not queueing at all. **Known residue, corrected after review:** `restore` (undo) walks a row back into `pending` without consulting the open row an agent's retry raised meanwhile, so dismiss → retry → undo still leaves two open rows. Approving both is NOT uniformly "refused out loud" — that holds only for the attended, parked and deferred-irreversible sub-cases, where the first row still occupies its index slot. On the **reversible unattended** path the first approval's `markReplayed` stamps `replayed_at`, the row LEAVES `decisions_v1_authorised_unconsumed`, the second claim finds the slot free and **the executor runs a second time, silently** — the same double send this card removes, reached by another route. Both halves pinned by `RESIDUE:` canary tests asserting executor invocation counts. **Taking the lock in `restore` would NOT close it** (the two writes touch different rows; `restore` never checks for a colliding open row, so both end `pending` in either order) — closing it needs a collapse at approve time or a `restore` that declines to reopen over a collision, which are rulings on what undo means. Left open deliberately, filed as its own card. | `INSERT … WHERE NOT EXISTS` (rejected — under READ COMMITTED neither transaction sees the other's uncommitted row; both insert). SERIALIZABLE (rejected — trades this for serialization failures the caller must then handle at a fail-closed gate). |
| 2026-08-23 | The collapse key is **(agent_id, call_fingerprint) AND owner_user_id**, over the OPEN statuses (`pending`, `stale`) only — deliberately NOT scoped to the conversation. | It matches `decisions_v1_authorised_unconsumed`'s own key, which is what makes the refusal branch unreachable rather than merely rarer: that index has no conversation in it, so two open rows in two of one person's threads are two cards for ONE authorisation and approving the second is precisely the refusal. The owner narrowing is the one deviation and it protects against a lost hold: reads are owner-scoped, so handing user B the id of user A's row on a shared team agent gives B a question they cannot see, answer or dismiss. That leaves a real residue — two owners of one team agent still collide, loudly — pinned by a test rather than left to be rediscovered. Cross-thread reuse means the in-thread card stays in the thread that asked first; the Today queue is not per-thread, so the question is still answerable. It also costs the second thread its NARRATION when the two threads differ in attendance — a hold raised by a routine and reused by a live web thread is replayed by the host, so that thread's warm agent is never told. One call, one card, no lost hold; pinned by a canary test. | Scope to the conversation (rejected — leaves the collision, and the collision is the bug). Ignore the owner (rejected — a hold nobody can answer is worse than a duplicate). |
| 2026-08-23 | On reuse the gate **does not re-fire `decisions:raised`**, and logs `decision_hold_reused` instead. | The event means "a new question is waiting" and the SSE subscriber turns it into a card; firing it for a row already on the queue draws the same card twice, which is the visible half of the bug. The log line is the operator's trace. | Fire it again (rejected — duplicate card). Fire nothing at all (rejected — no trace of a path that silently changes which decision id a runner is holding). |
| 2026-08-23 | **What TASK-253 (#448) already covers vs what this adds**, recorded because the card understated the bug: #448 classifies the pg `23505` into `DuplicateAuthorisationError` and reports `CLAIM_REFUSED_DETAIL` instead of swallowing it — verified still working on the attended path. But the index carries `replayed_at IS NULL`, so on the UNATTENDED host-replay path the first approval frees the slot and the second approval never hits the index: measured pre-fix, the executor ran **twice** for one call shape with both rows reading `executed`. The card's "absorbs a unique violation" describes only the not-yet-sent paths. This card removes the duplicate, so both outcomes become unreachable from a duplicate hold; nothing in #448 was weakened. | — |

## 2026-08-23 — TASK-266 `decisions:count` with a window (the rail's counter, in one read)

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-23 | The **window is a trailing time range over `createdAt`** — `{ userId, agentId?, since }`, `since` REQUIRED and INCLUSIVE, no upper end, **no status filter**. | Designed against what `readCounters` actually asks, not against the word "window". The rail draws one row whose shipped sentence is "decisions this agent raised for you in the last 7 days, whatever you decided — including the ones that expired": one owner, one agent, one lower time bound, every status. A trailing bound is the whole question ("recently" is always "then → now", and a decision cannot be raised in the future, so the missing end would filter nothing). `since` is required because omitting it would have to mean an unbounded scan of a growing table AND a number with no stated period beside it, which is the exact drift §4.4's counter table exists to prevent. | (a) `{ windowDays: number }` — REJECTED, puts the host's clock inside the plugin and makes the caller's own `now()` unusable as a test seam. (b) Add `before` for symmetry with `decisions:recent-receipts-for-agent` — REJECTED as YAGNI: no caller has a historical window, and the receipts hook needs `before` because it PAGES. (c) Add a `statuses` set — REJECTED, and not only on YAGNI: see the next row, where its absence is load-bearing. |
| 2026-08-23 | **`decisions:count` does NOT sweep.** Expiry stays exactly where it was: the maintenance timer, the `decisions:sweep` hook, and (still) inline on `decisions:list`. | And the staleness bound is **zero**, not "small" — which is only true because the count names no status. `expireDue` rewrites `status` and stamps `resolved_at`; it never touches `created_at` and never deletes a row. A count filtered on `created_at` across every status therefore returns the identical number either side of a sweep, so sweeping first would buy nothing and cost a table write per render per agent. Pinned as arithmetic in `store.test.ts` ("gives the same answer either side of a sweep") rather than asserted in prose. THE COROLLARY IS THE WARNING: this argument is a property of THIS query. The first status filter added here makes the count something expiry can move, and whoever adds one inherits the staleness question this read gets to skip. | (a) Sweep inside `count` — REJECTED, reintroduces the write the card exists to remove for a number that cannot observe it. (b) Move the sweep off `decisions:list` too — REJECTED, that is TASK-246's call to make, and the queue read is the one surface where a `pending` card that has actually expired is a button that lies. |
| 2026-08-23 | The route's `ALL_DECISION_STATUSES` enumeration is **deleted**, not kept alongside. | It existed only to spell out the walk, and it was a standing undercount hazard: a status added to `@ax/decisions` and not mirrored in `channel-web` would have quietly claimed an agent bothered you less than it did. Naming no status removes the list that could go stale. The rail test that pinned the enumeration against the wire union is replaced by one asserting the route sends NO `status` key at all. It also closes a second, smaller hole the walk had — a decision raised mid-walk into an already-walked status was missed; one statement has no "already walked". | Keep the constant for other callers — REJECTED, it had none. |
| 2026-08-23 | A non-numeric `count` on the wire is reported as **`status: 'failed'`**, never coerced to `0`. | Same rule the rest of the rail follows (I3 / H7): an empty answer here is a claim about how much an agent bothered you, and "the read broke" must never render as "nothing happened". `Number(out.count) \|\| 0` would have turned a broken producer into a confident zero. | Trust the bus's `returns` schema — REJECTED, it only binds the producer that declares one; the route duck-types every hook on this surface. |

| Date | Decision | Rationale | Alternatives |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-23 | TASK-274's bounded retry lives in **`useConversationDecisions`**, NOT in `useDecisionQueue` where `InThreadApprovals`' comment had promised it. Keeping it out of `useDecisionQueue` also leaves `/workspace` untouched — `TodayView` already renders `queue.error` with its own Try again. | (a) In `useDecisionQueue` unconditionally — REJECTED: changes `/workspace` too and burns attempts before there is anywhere to show a row. (b) An interval/poll — REJECTED: this read is ambient on the default surface, so a poll multiplies an outage by every open tab for a queue that is otherwise event-driven. (c) A `visibilitychange`/`focus` listener — REJECTED as a separate product behaviour, not this card. |
| 2026-08-23 | The retry budget is per OUTAGE and is refilled by **no click and no frame** — a manual `Try again` or a new `decisionRaised` frame fires a read but hands back no automatic attempts. (A successful read resets it; so does leaving the state it is about — a null conversation, or `kind` flipping to `expired`. Corrected by re-review Nit 2, which caught the first draft's "nothing else refills it" as an absolute with two unlisted exceptions.) | It makes "bounded" a claim about the whole failure episode rather than per trigger, which is the only version that cannot be turned into a poll by a user leaning on a button or by a noisy stream of frames. Documented on `READ_RETRY_DELAYS_MS`. | Refill on any externally-triggered read — REJECTED: an SSE storm during an outage would then be an unbounded retry loop wearing a different name. |
| 2026-08-23 | `DECISION_READ_RETRYING` ships — "We couldn’t check what’s waiting. Trying again. The button stays because it is the same action either way and never a lie: a person watching for an approval can have the answer now instead of waiting out a back-off, and hiding the only control at the moment somebody wants it, then popping it back, is worse than the mild redundancy. It also keeps the contract `in-thread-approvals.test.tsx:181` already pinned. | Hide the button while retrying — REJECTED (takes the control away exactly when it is wanted, and breaks a shipped test's contract for no gain). | 2026-08-23 | TASK-274: the retry tally increments when an attempt actually **fires**, not when one is **scheduled**. | Scheduling is not idempotent: React re-runs the effect on every new `error` object, which a click or a frame does on every failure. Added on review: (E) a DUPLICATED rail row, (F) the rail gaining a row the intersection does not support (`builtins.todo-write`). | The reviewer named F as the mirror image of A–D and worth an explicit line; E only became detectable after the de-dup fix. ## 2026-08-23 — TASK-243: refused the card's "unify the two rejecters" option; shipped comment-only

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | Rewrite eight false comments in `packages/ipc-core/src/handlers/workspace-commit-notify.ts` and change **zero** code lines. Explicitly decline the card's own acceptance option, *"or the two rejecters unified if that is simpler."* |
| **Rationale** | The two `recoverable:false` branches differ on purpose. Author-verify omits `discardPaths` because authorship is unestablished — no path set the bundle names can be trusted, so "keep the rest" is not a coherent offer and the whole-tree `--hard` is intentional. The pre-apply veto branch *conditionally adds* `discardPaths` from `Rejection.offendingPaths` (TASK-287, #464). Unifying them has only two outcomes: strip the veto's scoping (reverts #464 and restores the routine `CLAUDE.md` collateral it fixed), or let a **forged** bundle receive scoped discards (a tampered bundle survives). They also differ in source — a hook result vs. a thrown error with a fixed sanitized string. The comment recording this is the only record of the reason and is preserved verbatim. |
| **Alternatives** | Unify and add a flag: same hazard with a switch on it. Extract a shared body: the two bodies share three fields (`accepted`, `reason`, `recoverable`) of a four-field union; the shared part is `{accepted:false, recoverable:false}`, which is not worth a helper and would put the security-relevant difference behind an argument. |

## 2026-08-23 — TASK-243: no test accompanies a comment-only PR, said plainly

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | Ship with no new test and state the reasoning in the PR body rather than inventing one. |
| **Rationale** | The Bug Fix Policy asks for the test that would have caught the bug. For prose there is none — no assertion reads a comment, and a test that asserted on comment *text* would pin the wording, not the correctness, and would rot with the next edit. Writing one to look compliant is worse than saying so. |
| **Alternatives** | A lint rule / doc-comment test: real but a much larger piece of work than this card, and it would have to know what the code means, not just what the comment says. Left unfiled here deliberately — the card that claims this handler has no tests is already wrong (it has 599 lines of them), so the follow-up is to correct that card, not to add coverage. |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-262: the freshness reach-fold gate goes on the FOLD, never on the predicate

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | `capability-freshness.ts`'s `catalogToken` folds each referenced connector's resolved reach into the digest **only when `bus.hasService('connectors:resolve')`**, and when the hook is absent it hashes the pre-TASK-262 shape byte for byte (no `reach` key at all). The `hasService` check sits *inside* `catalogToken`, not at the top of the capture handler. |
| **Rationale** | The sibling producer `packages/tool-connector-propose/src/freshness.ts:202` returns `{predicate:null}` when the hook is missing — correct **there**, because the connector registry is the only world that producer reads. Copying that pattern here (the default move for anyone reading the two files side by side) would blank this predicate and **delete the working catalog guard in every connector-less preset**. The catalog entry is still a world worth guarding without `@ax/connectors`. Byte-identical fallback additionally means no in-flight `request_capability` row in such a preset is staled by this PR. |
| **Alternatives** | Whole-predicate gate (rejected — deletes a guard). Always emit a `reach: []` key (rejected — stales every connector-less preset's in-flight rows for no information). Make `connectors:resolve` a hard `calls` dep (rejected — invariant 5 / breaks stripped presets). |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-262: the fold resolves in PARALLEL and throws where the executor swallows

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | `resolvedReach` uses `Promise.all` over the connector ids, leaves `timeoutMs` at 3 s/10 s, maps a clean `PluginError{code:'not-found'}` to an `absent` sentinel, and **re-throws every other resolve failure** — the opposite of the executor's per-connector `catch {}` in `request-capability.ts`. |
| **Rationale** | The two halves of the guard fail in OPPOSITE directions on budget overrun: `@ax/decisions`' `CAPTURE_BUDGET_MS` (3 s) makes capture fail **OPEN** (row written with no predicate, claiming no guard), and `CHECK_BUDGET_MS` (10 s) makes check fail **CLOSED** (spurious stale). So a serial fan-out over N connectors is how a two-connector skill quietly loses its guard; parallel makes the fold cost one round trip regardless of N and needs no larger budget. On the throw: the executor must still draw a card, so dropping an unreadable connector is right for it; a freshness producer doing the same would report "unchanged" for a world it failed to read, letting a transient blip authorise a replay. |
| **Alternatives** | Serial loop + raise `timeoutMs` (rejected — a producer cannot raise the pre-call IPC ceiling, so it would just move the failure). `Promise.allSettled` + swallow (rejected — that is the executor's posture, and it is wrong for a guard). |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-262: digest membership is "resolve returns it and it grants reach"

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | The reach shape digests keyMode, hosts, credential slot NAMES, npm, pypi, **`mcpServers`** and **`services`** — including `env` as sorted key/value pairs. `usageNote` and `credentialPlan` stay out. Set-like arrays are deduped+sorted; `args` keeps its order. |
| **Rationale** | The sibling omits `mcpServers` (and `services`) even though `connectors:resolve` returns both; that is a blind spot, not a precedent — an MCP server or a dev-service image is reach. `env` values are in because an env value is how either gets re-pointed somewhere else with every host string unchanged; only the sha256 is persisted, so nothing sensitive is stored or logged. `args` order is meaning (`['--allow','x']` ≠ `['x','--allow']`), so sorting it would collapse two different worlds. |
| **Alternatives** | Canonical-JSON the whole `capabilities` object (rejected — a generic recursive sort would either reorder `args` or leave set-like lists order-sensitive). env keys only (rejected — misses a real reach change). Mirror the sibling exactly (rejected — inherits its blind spot). |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-262: the predicate's `label` DOES follow the fold (initial call reversed on review)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | The label now branches: `the "<skillId>" capability and the connectors it reaches` when the reach fold ran, `the "<skillId>" entry in the capability catalog` when it did not. **This reverses my first call**, which was to leave it alone; `ax-code-reviewer` pushed back and was right. |
| **Rationale** | The label completes "checked against: …" on the row a human reads. When a CONNECTOR moves and the catalog entry does not, "the entry in the capability catalog" sends them to inspect the entry, where they find nothing changed — worse than saying nothing. Branching is not per-preset inconsistency: a connector-less preset genuinely checked less, and should say so. **My length objection was factually wrong** — `@ax/decisions`' `fenceLine` truncates at `LABEL_MAX_CHARS` with an ellipsis rather than dropping the label, so a pathological 128-char skillId degrades gracefully. |
| **Alternatives** | Leave it (rejected on review — understating what was checked on a consent surface is the defect this epic is cleaning up). Re-read `hasService` at the label site (rejected — `catalogToken` now returns `{value, foldedReach}` so the label CANNOT desync from the gate; a second read would work today and rot the first time the condition changes). |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-314: rejected the card's own proposed fix for the `waitFor` finding

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | The card said to replace "`waitFor` gets its first look in on a later macrotask" with "`waitFor` runs inside React's `act()`, which drains microtasks and flushes commits before resolving". I kept the correction of the first half and **rejected the proposed replacement as false**, writing the mechanism I measured instead: the first check is synchronous, and what puts committed state behind the following assertions is that the configured `asyncWrapper` awaits a `setTimeout(…, 0)` before resolving. |
| **Rationale** | `@testing-library/react`'s `asyncWrapper` calls `setReactActEnvironment(false)` for the duration of the wait — its own source comment says "We just want to run `waitFor` without IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT". A throwaway probe (deleted before commit) measured `IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT` **false** inside the callback, the first check on the synchronous tick, and a `setTimeout(…, 0)` queued before the call running before it resolved. So `act()` is the one thing the wait provably does *not* run inside. The original line's macrotask instinct was right about *resolution* and wrong about the *first look*; the card had it wrong in the other direction. Writing the card's version would have put a third false claim into the same bullet this card exists to fix. |
| **Alternatives** | Write the card's version as specified (rejected — measurably false). Escalate to Needs Input (rejected — the card's *conclusion* and the other four findings were unaffected, and the truth was cheap to measure directly). |

|---|---|
| **Decision** | Wrap the `docker pull` in a 3-attempt backoff retry, despite TASK-316 having deliberately *removed* a 3x retry from the chart suite's helm fetch. |
| **Rationale** | TASK-316's retry was harmful for a specific reason, not a general one: the empty index it retried around was **self-inflicted by concurrent writers**, so every attempt fired another `--force-update` into the same contended files and amplified the race. A single serialized `docker pull` in one CI step has no competing writer and therefore no race to amplify — only a genuinely flaky remote, which is what a bounded retry is for. Stated explicitly in the step comment and the PR because a reviewer citing "316 removed its retry" would be misapplying it. |
| **Alternatives** | Naked single pull (rejected — moves the flake to a named step instead of removing it). Unbounded retry (rejected — turns a dead registry into a job timeout). |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-317: acceptance is mechanical, not statistical

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | Do **not** claim N-consecutive-green-runs as the acceptance evidence, even though the card specified it. |
| **Rationale** | The failure has exactly **one** observation, and the 8 `main` runs preceding this work were already green **without** the fix — so consecutive green runs cannot distinguish the fix from the baseline. The real proof is mechanical and checkable by reading the installed library: `pullImage` returns early on a purely local `dockerode.getImage(name).inspect()` and nothing in this repo sets `force`, so a resident image is never manifest-checked. The mechanical argument is only as complete as the image inventory it covers, which is what the Ryuk finding below corrected — a mechanical claim can be sound in its reasoning and still false in its scope. Green runs bound the added cost and show no regression; they are not the proof. |
| **Alternatives** | Report green-run counts as acceptance (rejected — dressing up an n=1 with statistics it does not have). Add a unit test asserting the flake is gone (rejected — there is nothing in-process to assert; the behaviour is CI-environment shaped, hence the source-shape guard instead). |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-317: DISABLE the Ryuk reaper in CI rather than pre-pulling it

| | |
|---|---|
| **Decision** | Set `TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED: 'true'` on the CI `test` job, instead of adding `testcontainers/ryuk:0.14.0` to the pre-pull list. The guard asserts the pairing (reaper off **or** image pre-pulled), so both configurations are legal and only "neither" fails. |
| **Rationale** | Reviewer finding, and it was correct: testcontainers starts the reaper on every `.start()`, so the first draft closed the postgres vector while leaving an identical registry-blip vector open — and said in comments that it was closed. Disabling beats pre-pulling on two counts. The reaper exists to clean up containers leaked after a session dies, and a GitHub-hosted runner is destroyed at the end of the job, so it buys nothing there. And its tag is pinned by the *installed* testcontainers, so a pre-pulled copy would drift on every dependency bump with nothing able to police it — the guard's source scan can never see a library-internal image. Disabling keeps the policed list at exactly one image, which is also the model the rest of the guard assumes. |
| **Alternatives** | Pre-pull the reaper image (rejected as the primary fix for the drift reason above, but deliberately left *legal* by the guard, because a future need for real reaping in CI should not require rewriting the guard). Leave it and soften the comments to admit the gap (rejected — the card's whole goal is that a registry blip cannot fail a suite; documenting a known-open vector as acceptable fails the card). Both belt-and-braces (rejected — contradictory: disabling means nothing pulls the image, so pre-pulling it too is dead weight the guard would then have to permit forever). |

## 2026-08-24 — TASK-319: the per-slot fold digests WHERE a grant is exchanged, not just what it permits

| **Decision** | `capability-freshness.ts`'s `slotShapes` now folds `clientId`, `clientSecretRef`, `authServerUrl` and `tokenUrl` alongside `{slot, kind, server, scopes}`, and the `services` map folds a new `healthcheckShape()`. Digesting only the former let an admin re-point `authServerUrl` with the reach token byte-identical — verified by probe before the work started, and reproduced as a failing test before the fix — so an approved capability kept its approval while pointing somewhere else. Same class of fact as `scopes`, same guard. `healthcheck` is the most reach-shaped field on a dev service: an `exec` probe becomes the pod's `startupProbe` in `sandbox-k8s/src/pod-spec.ts`, i.e. a command run inside the container. |
| **Alternatives** | Gate the whole predicate on `hasService` like the sibling producer `tool-connector-propose/src/freshness.ts` (rejected — that producer reads ONE world, this one reads TWO; copying its line deletes the catalog guard in every connector-less preset. This is the second time the same trap has been written down and it nearly shipped once). Widen `@ax/connectors`' schema (rejected — unnecessary, all five were already declared and `ResolveOutputSchema` round-trips them; asserted in `oauth-slot.test.ts` rather than assumed, because `returns:` is a `z.object` and a `z.object` strips what it does not declare). Hash the whole `ResolveOutput` (rejected — `usageNote` is prose, and staling an approval on a reworded blurb is how a guard that cries wolf gets clicked through; there is a negative test pinning that direction). |
